questions.stem: A scrapyard crane uses an electromagnet to pick up old cars. Why is an electromagnet used instead of a permanent magnet?

options.text: An electromagnet is always stronger than a permanent magnet
An electromagnet can be switched off to release the car when needed
Electromagnets do not need electricity to work

questions.explanation: The key advantage of an electromagnet is that it can be switched on and off by controlling the current. This allows the crane to pick up a car (current on) and then release it (current off). Permanent magnets can attract steel (C is wrong), and electromagnets do require electricity (D is wrong). While electromagnets can be very strong, the main reason here is controllability, not just strength (A).

questions.stem: A student wraps 50 turns of wire around a soft iron nail and connects it to a battery. The electromagnet picks up 12 paperclips. She then wraps 100 turns around the same nail using the same battery. Approximately how many paperclips would you expect the electromagnet to pick up?
questions.explanation: Increasing the number of turns on a solenoid increases the magnetic field strength. Doubling the number of turns (from 50 to 100) approximately doubles the field strength, so the electromagnet should pick up roughly twice as many paperclips (about 24). The field strength does not stay the same (B) or decrease (A) when more turns are added.

questions.stem: An electromagnet is made by winding wire around a core. Which core material would make the electromagnet lose its magnetism most quickly when the current is switched off?
questions.explanation: Soft iron is magnetically 'soft' -- it magnetises and demagnetises easily, making it ideal for electromagnets that need to be switched on and off. Steel is magnetically 'hard' and retains its magnetism after the current stops (A). Copper (C) and aluminium (D) are not magnetic materials and would not work as electromagnet cores at all.

questions.stem: A solenoid is connected to a DC power supply. Using the right-hand rule, a student determines the north pole is at the left end. Which change would reverse the position of the poles?

options.text: Adding more turns to the solenoid
Reversing the direction of the current

questions.explanation: The polarity of a solenoid (which end is north and which is south) depends on the direction of current flow. Reversing the current reverses the poles. Increasing the current (A) or adding more turns (B) would make the electromagnet stronger but not change which end is north. Inserting an iron core (D) strengthens the field but does not reverse polarity.

questions.stem: A relay uses a small current in one circuit to switch on a larger current in a separate circuit. Which component inside a relay is essential for this to work?

options.text: A permanent magnet that attracts the switch contacts
A transformer that steps up the voltage
An electromagnet that pulls a switch arm to close a second circuit
A capacitor that stores charge for the second circuit

questions.explanation: A relay contains an electromagnet. When a small current flows through the electromagnet's coil, it creates a magnetic field that pulls a pivoted switch arm, closing the contacts in a separate, high-current circuit. A permanent magnet (A) could not be switched on and off. A transformer (B) changes voltage but does not act as a switch. A capacitor (D) stores charge but is not the switching mechanism.
